title: An abelian subgroup admits an equivariant positive-multiple map
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected separated group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], where separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Let $i:A\hookrightarrow G$ be a central closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] with $A$ an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety]; central means that $i(A(R))$ commutes with $G(R)$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$. There exist a positive integer $n$ and a $k$-scheme morphism $\phi:G\to A$ such that, for every $k$-scheme $T$ and $g\in G(T)$, $a\in A(T)$, $$\phi(g\,i(a))=\phi(g)+[n]_A(a).$$ Here $[n]_A$ is multiplication by $n$ [def-sc-mult-n], and the equality is an equality of morphisms on the fibre product $G\times_kA$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. The morphism $\phi$ is not required to preserve the identity. No properness, affineness or commutativity assumption is imposed on $G$.

source.place: Proposition 8.23 and Lemma 8.22, printed pp.152–153. The positive integer is the degree n in the proof of Lemma 8.22 (n=1 in its rational-point case). No Stacks tag states this equivariant map theorem.

proof.text: Both $G$ and $A$ are nonempty, since they have identity sections. Apply [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] to each structure morphism and its identity section. Thus both are geometrically connected. Apply [lem-trf-smooth-connected-fibre-normal-integrality] over $\operatorname{Spec}k$ to conclude that $G_K$ and $A_K$ are integral for every field extension $K/k$. In particular $G$ and $A$ are geometrically integral. Moreover $A$ is commutative directly from the hypotheses: on any affine test scheme, centrality says $i(a)i(b)=i(b)i(a)$, and the monomorphism $i$ gives $a+b=b+a$. These identities glue over affine covers of arbitrary test schemes; evaluating at the identity of $A\times_kA$ proves commutativity as a group-scheme identity.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient] to $i:A\hookrightarrow G$. Obtain a separated finite-type $k$-scheme $Q$ and a flat surjective finitely presented map $p:G\to Q$. Its test-scheme coset criterion identifies
$$\theta:G\times_k A\longrightarrow G\times_QG,\qquad (g,a)\longmapsto(g,g\,i(a))$$
as an isomorphism. Indeed, for every $k$-scheme $T$, a pair $(g,h)$ in the kernel pair has a unique $a\in A(T)$ with $g^{-1}h=i(a)$; uniqueness uses the monomorphism $i$. This gives a natural inverse, hence a scheme inverse by [lem-galois-yoneda-fully-faithful]. The same criterion gives $p(g\,i(a))=p(g)$, as an equality of morphisms. No commutativity of $G$ is used.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Under $\theta$, the first projection $G\times_QG\to G$, which is the base change of $p$ along $p$, becomes $G\times_k A\to G$. It is smooth by [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2). The map $p$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact (it is finitely presented); [lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent] therefore makes $p$ smooth. Apply [lem-sbc-smooth-flat-surjective-source-descent] to $G\xrightarrow p Q\to\operatorname{Spec}k$: the first map is flat, surjective and locally finitely presented and the composite is smooth. Thus $Q$ is smooth over $k$. It is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-scheme-over-field-regular]. It is nonempty and connected as the continuous surjective image of the nonempty connected $G$. Hence [lem-sc-regular-connected-integral] makes $Q$ integral.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Let $\eta\in Q$ be the generic point, $K=\kappa(\eta)$ and $V=G\times_Q\operatorname{Spec}K$. By [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-base-change] and [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change], $V\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is flat and surjective. It is of finite type: finite presentation of $p$ is preserved by scalar extension, since finite algebra presentations tensor to finite presentations on affine charts. Pulling $\theta$ back gives $V\times_K A_K\simeq V\times_KV$ with the right translation action. By [lem-pc-proper-base-change](1),(2), $A_K$ is proper and smooth; properness includes separatedness and finite type. It is commutative and geometrically integral by step 1. Thus [lem-sfb-commutative-torsor-positive-weight], over the possibly imperfect field $K$, gives $n>0$ and $f_V:V\to A_K$ with $f_V(va)=f_V(v)+[n]a$ as morphisms on $V\times_K A_K$.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text: The surjective $p$ is dominant. The generic point $\xi$ of the integral $G$ therefore maps to $\eta$. The generic fibre $V$ is integral with generic point induced by $\xi$ and the same function field as $G$: on affine opens over $B=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset Q$, its charts are $\operatorname{Spec}((R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}C)$ for domains $C$ with injective $R\to C$, and have fraction field $k(G)$. Thus the composite $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{G,\xi}=\operatorname{Spec}k(G)\to V\xrightarrow{f_V}A_K\to A$ is a $k$-morphism. By [lem-sfb-local-ring-map-spread], applied with source $G$, base $\operatorname{Spec}k$ and target $A$, it extends to $f_U:U\to A$ on an open neighbourhood $U$ of $\xi$. Its hypotheses hold: $A$ is locally finite type, and $G$ is locally Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-scheme-over-field-regular]. The open $U$ is dense. Apply [lem-sfb-weil-extension-to-abelian-variety] to the smooth integral separated finite-type $G$ and $A$: obtain a morphism $\phi:G\to A$ extending $f_U$.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Let $\phi_\eta:V\to A_K$ be the base change over $Q$ of $(p,\phi):G\to Q\times_k A$. Both $\phi_\eta$ and $f_V$ agree on the canonical generic-point morphism $\operatorname{Spec}k(G)\to V$, by step 5 and the fibre-product universal property. That morphism has dense image, and $V$ is reduced by step 5. The target $A_K$ is separated over $K$. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-separated-dominant-ext], with $T=V$, $W=\operatorname{Spec}k(G)$, $Y=A_K$ and $S=\operatorname{Spec}K$, to get $\phi_\eta=f_V$ on all of $V$, not just at its generic point.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Put $X=G\times_k A$ and $q=p\circ\operatorname{pr}_1:X\to Q$. The projection $X\to G$ is smooth by [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2), so $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth by [lem-trf-smooth-composition]. It is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. Since $G$ and $A$ are geometrically integral, [lem-sc-geometrically-irreducible-product] makes $X$ irreducible; hence it is integral. The identity of $A$ gives a section of $X\to G$, so this projection is surjective and $q$ is dominant. Its generic fibre is canonically $X_\eta=V\times_K A_K$. Its image in $X$ is dense: the generic point of integral $X$ maps to $\eta$ under the dominant $q$ and factors through that fibre. This uses only the generic-point description of the fibre; it asserts no open-immersion property for a generic fibre.

source.place: Proposition 8.23, printed pp.152–153, proof; Lemma 8.22 and 8.18. Generic-point spreading and equality of scheme morphisms expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Consider the two $k$-morphisms $b,c:X\to A$ defined by $b(g,a)=\phi(g\,i(a))$ and $c(g,a)=\phi(g)+[n]_A(a)$. The action is over $Q$ by step 2. On $X_\eta=V\times_KA_K$, step 6 identifies $\phi_\eta$ with $f_V$, so step 4 gives $b|_{X_\eta}=c|_{X_\eta}$ as scheme morphisms. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-separated-dominant-ext] with reduced source $X$, dense-image morphism $X_\eta\to X$ and separated target $A/k$. It yields $b=c$ on $X$. Pulling this equality back along each $T\to X$ gives the required formula for every $k$-scheme $T$, including nonreduced ones. The integer is the positive $n$ of step 4, and the construction imposes no condition on $\phi(e_G)$.

tool_uses.why: Geometric connectedness from a rational identity section; generic scheme tool used for G and A, not a replacement of the unit route.
Only the generic smooth geometric-fibre integrality theorem over a field is used; no trace formula or duality input.
Yoneda converts the natural test-scheme inverse of the torsor kernel-pair map into a scheme inverse.
Smoothness under base change gives projections and A_K; properness under base change gives separated finite-type A_K.
Generic fpqc descent of smooth scheme morphisms for the homogeneous quotient.
Generic source descent of smoothness for Q/k, with p flat surjective and locally finitely presented.
Generic regularity and local Noetherianity of smooth field schemes, for Q and G.
Generic integrality of a nonempty connected regular scheme, applied to Q.
Generic preservation of flatness for the quotient generic fibre.
Generic preservation of surjectivity for the quotient generic fibre.
Generic composition of smooth scheme maps to see G times A is smooth over k.
Generic geometric reducedness of smooth fibres, to make G times A reduced.
Generic geometric irreducibility of products over a field, for G times A.

The statement is unchanged: k algebraically closed, A a central abelian closed subgroup, n>0, equality of morphisms on G×A. The delivery adds no new nodes. All 18 cited statements were read and their hypotheses checked. Step 1: geometric connectedness from the identity section (lem-sbc), then geometric integrality from lem-trf-smooth-connected-fibre-normal-integrality with B=Spec k; A is commutative directly from centrality, on affine test schemes. Step 2: the homogeneous quotient and its coset criterion give the inverse of θ, made a scheme map by Yoneda. Step 3: smooth source descent makes Q smooth, hence regular, connected and integral. The fpqc-descent clause there is correct but not used later (harmless). Step 4: V is a flat, surjective, finite-type A_K-torsor, and A_K meets every hypothesis of commutative-torsor-positive-weight, including geometric integrality over K. Steps 5–6: V is the localization at the generic point, the map spreads from the local ring and the Weil extension applies to G, and the dense-image extension gives φ_η=f_V. Steps 7–8: X=G×A is smooth, reduced and irreducible, X_η has dense image, and b=c by the dense-image extension with A/k separated. Small cases A=G (Q a point, n=1), A=0 and G=A×H all work. Duplicate check: lem-sfb-abelian-inclusion-multiple-retraction is the special case G=A, not a duplicate and not cited, so there is no cycle. Batch-5 citations (lem-trf smooth-fibre integrality, smooth-fpqc-base-descent, smooth-composition, and through the existing nodes def-trf-scheme-algebraic-space and lem-trf-smooth-geometrically-normal) are generic scheme facts or definitions, not steps of the trace formula or Poincaré duality.
